I also support offering Puerto Rico statehood if—and only if—Puerto Ricans clearly choose it through a fair, definitive self-determination vote. In both cases, the core principle is equal representation and consent of the governed.

Online learning is not a suitable full replacement for traditional in-person education. It can match or exceed in-person outcomes for some learners, subjects, and contexts, but it consistently struggles to replicate hands-on practice, spontaneous interaction, and the social development benefits of being physically together. The best stance is that online learning is a strong complement and, in some cases, an effective alternative—not a universal substitute.

Online learning is not a full replacement for traditional in-person education, though it can be an excellent alternative in many cases. It works best for self-directed learners and subjects that don’t require hands-on practice, while in-person settings are usually stronger for labs, clinical skills, social development, and immediate feedback. The most effective approach for most learners is a blended model that combines online flexibility with periodic face-to-face instruction.

Online learning is not a full replacement for traditional in-person education, though it can be equally effective for many learners and subjects. In-person settings still offer advantages in hands-on practice, spontaneous discussion, mentoring, and social development that are hard to replicate online. My stance: the best approach is hybrid—use online learning where it works best, and keep in-person education where it adds unique value.

Online learning is not a full replacement for traditional in-person education. It works well as a complement or for specific learners and contexts, but in-person schooling provides stronger real-time interaction, social development, and hands-on support that many students need. The best approach is a blended model that uses online tools to enhance—not substitute—face-to-face learning.

Online learning is not a suitable full replacement for traditional in-person education for most students and most subjects. It can match or exceed in-person outcomes in specific cases (motivated adult learners, well-designed courses, some theory-heavy topics), but it often falls short on hands-on practice, social development, and consistent engagement. The best approach is hybrid: use online tools for flexibility and personalization while keeping in-person instruction for interaction, mentoring, labs, and community.

I oppose keeping the penny in circulation. It costs more to make than it’s worth, is inefficient to use in transactions, and largely ends up unused. Prices can be rounded to the nearest five cents (as in other countries) with minimal impact on consumers.

I’m in favor of discontinuing the penny in regular circulation. It costs more to produce than it’s worth and adds friction to cash transactions without providing meaningful purchasing power. Keep it legal tender for redemptions, but stop minting it and shift to rounding at the register for cash payments.

I’m in favor of discontinuing the penny in everyday circulation.  
It costs more to produce than it’s worth and adds friction to cash transactions for minimal practical benefit.  
Prices can still be set precisely, with totals rounded at checkout (as other countries do) while keeping the cent for accounting.

I support discontinuing the U.S. penny and removing it from active circulation.  
It costs more to produce than it’s worth, adds time and handling costs for businesses and consumers, and its purchasing power is effectively negligible.  
Prices can be rounded to the nearest five cents at the register (as Canada does) while electronic payments remain exact, minimizing any real downside.

I support retiring the U.S. penny from circulation. It costs more than one cent to produce, adds time and handling costs for consumers and businesses, and provides minimal practical value in everyday transactions. Prices can still be set precisely, with cash totals rounded to the nearest five cents while electronic payments remain exact.
